rv.q: It Hot is a delight from start to finish.
What could have been a dated drag farce ends up as a show that many will like immensely — a musical filled with fun, energy and heart.
“It Hot,” which opened at the Shubert Theatre tonight, manages to speak to the moment with sizzle, polish and expert understanding of how to please a crowd.

That’s a pretty high standard, after all, and in its staging (by Casey Nicholaw), its revamped plot (by Matthew López and Amber Ruffin) and especially its songs (by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman), “It Hot” clears the bar handily.
You'll leave this show with a smile on your face, and why not?
Without it, there is no surprise, intellectually or emotionally, and that is the case here, even though that original film was full of shocks and wonders.
This fizzy adaptation of the Billy Wilder film classic is a crowd-pleasing musical that knows how to work an audience
The show is a fizzy, feel-good entertainment that delivers plenty of laughs and some unexpectedly touching moments.
By the end of it, all I could think is, Well, this is most of the way to being an incredible musical.
It’s easier to note all the ways the show doesn’t do anything wrong than the ways it executes new ideas of its own.
However, even if you go in totally cold — “Who’s Jack Lemmon?” God forbid — the show still disappoints as a stand-alone piece of theater.
If you’re a sucker for fast-paced glamour executed in high style, this is the one for you.
Whether you like it hot, cold, or even in the pot, nine days old, you’re probably going to like this show.
It's a guaranteed good night on Broadway, a glorious throwback that also manages to retrofit a well-known story for today.
It Hot is a wildly entertaining farce from start to finish.

And yet here comes It Hot, blazing a three-alarm fire with charm and wit to remind us of the joys that beautiful people, electric performances, exciting choreography and foot-stomping, finger-snapping, neck-pulsing music can inspire.
I imagine you'll make your own connections while viewing what is sure to be Broadway's next huge hit.

With the exception of the lively title song, Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman’s (“Hairspray”) big band-style score is derivative and serviceable at best. But taken on the whole, 'It Hot' is more than worth celebrating.
It Hot is a booze-soaked, boisterous good time from start to finish.
By delivering its pointed messages with such virtuosity and sheer spunk, “It Hot” manages to burn more brightly than most musicals of its kind.

“After a few months in which the new musicals have seemingly suffered from pernicious anemia, It Hot finds new vigor in roaring, raucous musical comedy. An old-style show with a new-style point of view, it updates Billy Wilder's vintage film farce with a nod to today's sensibilities.
It Hot has everything a Broadway musical should have: a superb cast, a great score, terrific choreography and the highest production values.
For the most part, It Hot succeeds in its aim of simply entertaining its audiences with those two most glorious words in the English language.
...Natasha Katz’s warm lighting create the perfect atmosphere for this joyfully ridiculous show. Despite its occasional lapses into preachiness, it’s a really Hot time.

Indeed, acceptance is the key to just sitting back in your seat and embracing all the great stuff onstage in “It Hot” -- even if this overstuffed show sometimes feels that it should have been renamed “A Lot.”
Whatever puzzles there are in story and character in the Broadway show are swept along by the wonderful dancing and music that keeps the show rattling along.
That’s correct, if not exactly thrilling theater.
Never has more been way too much.
Whether you leave feeling entertained or overwhelmed probably depends on how eager you are for a fun time.
The music by Marc Shaiman and lyrics by Scott Wittman and Shaiman are smart and enhance the story, not just dropped in for a pause.
Well, you could have knocked me over with a feather because I will forgive the flaws of It Hot as a theatrical experience to embrace the overwhelming authenticity.
Its creators desire to not offend anybody is actually more offensive than they think, tiptoeing when they should land with both feet hard.

cn.t: Critics praise this fizzy, crowd-pleasing adaptation for its razzle-dazzle choreography and energetic performances, though some find it exhausting or heavy-handed in updating the classic film's gender politics for modern sensibilities.

sg.ra: Shubert's orchestra rake is shallow, so the center aisle seats and rows in the low center (roughly E-L) give the cleanest unobstructed view without relying on being lifted over people's heads. Patrons repeatedly call out Row G center as 'the best seat in the house' and flag Row Q as the point where the mezzanine overhang starts to clip the very top of the stage.
sg.rr: A-R (front-to-mid); Q can start to feel the overhang

sg.ra: Orchestra Left sections include rush-priced partial-view seats — the trade is a clipped stage-right view for significantly lower pricing than center orchestra.
sg.rr: A-T (multiple reviews across the full front-to-rear span; rear rows marked partial view)

sg.ra: Front mezzanine center at the Shubert is the most-praised section in this dataset: patrons repeatedly call Row A 'best seats in the house' and note the mezzanine is unusually close to the stage because the house is wider than deep. The critical cutoff is explicit in the sourced Reddit advice — 'I wouldn't go much further back than row F in the mezz' — because the balcony overhang above starts clipping the top of the stage from roughly row G onward.
sg.rr: A-F (front rows unanimously recommended; avoid G+)

sg.ra: Skip at any price above deep-discount: Mezz Left Row A has a Shubert-specific hazard patrons repeatedly flag — a front rail / metal bar / banner that sits in the eye-line and requires shorter guests to dodge or sit unnaturally straight for the full runtime. Deep on the aisle side (row A27+) the proscenium box itself cuts off stage right, and the rider head-to-head with Mezzanine Right explicitly favors the opposite side here because 'a lot of action happens on the left side and I had to lean across.' Row B onward is tolerable but the front row — the only reason to pay premium — is the compromised row.
sg.rr: A-B (most photos); full section goes to row K

sg.ra: The padded velvet front-rail barrier on Mezz R Row A is a distinctive Shubert feature — patrons lean into it as a forearm rest rather than fight it. The section-specific tradeoff: Row B actually rates higher than Row A in direct rider comparisons here because the Shubert's aggressive mezz rise means Row B looks cleanly over the Row A patrons, so don't over-pay for A.

Shubert's balcony is the theater's weakest bucket per both riders and Reddit. The section-specific quirk: the balcony's front railing has a 'wide ledge' / light boxes that sit high enough to block the front of the stage — short patrons (≤5'4") are told to bring a cushion, and every rider reports leaning forward to see action downstage. Combine that with the 'steeply raked' upper tier and patrons describe it as 'watching the show in miniature.'

The front row of side balcony is the Shubert's genuine value play — a single Mockingbird patron posted 'Definitely worth $69' four consecutive times across A3-A9, and a Hell's Kitchen rider describes Balcony Row A as 'felt more like a front mezzanine' because it isn't yet steep there. The tradeoff unique to this section: deep-left seats (A25/27) hit a hard partial-view wall, and Row B onward sits behind a railing multiple patrons flag as 'very in the way.' Buy A, not B.
sg.rr: A (front row only; rows B+ get worse sight lines and railing obstruction)
